_note: TEST SLICE, 12 of 212 entries, one or two per class. Written after the robot-actuators and robot-sensors attempt failed: generated illustration is unreliable whenever the subject is only identifiable from an internal engagement (meshing teeth, brushes on a commutator, coaxial alignment), because precise part-to-part contact is what these models get wrong. Manufacturing processes should survive because each one reads as a distinct external silhouette, so every prompt here describes a recognizable setup seen from outside, with the workpiece and the tool clearly separated, and asks for no cutaways and no exploded assemblies. Anchor is 15, sand casting. Do not name copper anywhere: the house palette is steel-blue accents only.
_partNote: Class images for the explorer tiles. These render about 74px tall, so every prompt asks for one bold centered object with a simple silhouette and no fine detail. Subjects are deliberately chosen to be static or to involve one simple contact, because the 12-entry test showed that convergence, immersion, enclosure and shaped cavities all come back wrong. A class with no usable image is simply left out; the tile renders as it always did.
style: Minimalist technical illustration, the style of a precise patent drawing crossed with an isometric product sketch. Uniform-weight dark slate-gray ink linework with sparse, muted steel-blue accent shading (hex 4E7AA8) on a plain very light warm-gray background (hex F2F3F1). Three-quarter isometric view, single centered subject, generous margins. No text, no labels, no callouts, no logos, no humans, no background scenery, no drop shadows. Clean, engineered, calm. Strictly two colors plus the background: dark slate-gray line and muted steel-blue fill. Every material is drawn in that same palette. Absolutely no copper, brass, bronze, gold, orange, red, yellow or green anywhere, even where the real object would be that color. Favor open, airy linework with large unfilled light areas over heavy solid gray shading; the drawing should read as line art, not as a rendered solid model. Draw the setup as seen from outside, as a whole machine or workstation. Do not draw a cutaway, a section view or an exploded assembly. Keep the part count low and leave clear space between separate objects rather than making them interlock.

prompts.2: A rolling mill stand seen from the side: two large horizontal rolls stacked one above the other in a heavy rectangular frame, with a long flat metal strip entering the gap between them from the left and leaving thinner and longer to the right. The strip is a single continuous ribbon and is the full width of the rolls. Massive frame, simple shapes.
prompts.15: A sand casting setup: a rectangular two-part sand mold box sitting on the floor with a visible parting line around its middle, a tapered pouring cup and a riser standing up from its top face, and a long-handled foundry ladle tipped above the cup with a thin stream of metal falling into it. The ladle is clearly separate from and above the mold.
prompts.26: An injection molding machine seen from the side: a long horizontal barrel with a hopper standing on top of it feeding pellets down, a clamping unit at the far end holding two thick platens together, and a molded part with a small runner tree resting on a conveyor just below the open clamp. Long, low and horizontal.
prompts.45: A forging press: a heavy vertical frame with a massive upper die descending onto a lower die block, and a short thick glowing billet held between them being squashed outward, with a thin ring of flash spreading at the parting line. Emphasize the mass of the press and the small size of the workpiece.
prompts.65: A drill press: a vertical column carrying a motor head at the top, a chuck holding a single long twist drill with visible helical flutes pointing straight down, and a flat rectangular workpiece clamped on the table below with the drill just entering it. Chips curl away from the hole.
prompts.83: A waterjet cutting table: a flat wide slatted tank with a gantry bridge spanning it, a small cutting head hanging from the gantry with a fine jet leaving its nozzle, and a flat plate lying on the slats with an intricate curved profile part being cut free from it. The jet is a thin straight line.
prompts.100: A directed-energy deposition head: a robot arm carrying a nozzle assembly angled down at a thick metal substrate, with several fine powder streams converging from the nozzle onto one small bright melt pool, and a raised bead of deposited metal already built up in a line behind it. The convergence point is the focus.
prompts.137: An electron-beam welding chamber: a boxy vacuum chamber with a thick viewport window on the front and an electron gun column mounted vertically on its roof, with two heavy plates butted together on a rotary table inside and a narrow straight beam running down from the gun to the joint line.
prompts.175: An electroplating tank: an open rectangular tank of solution with a rack of flat parts hanging into it from a bus bar above, and two flat anode plates hanging parallel on either side, all suspended from the same bar. A small rectifier box stands beside the tank with two leads running to the bars.
prompts.184: A photolithography stepper: a tall rectangular machine body with an illumination column on top, a flat rectangular mask plate held horizontally in a frame partway down, a projection lens barrel below it, and a round silicon wafer on a flat stage at the bottom directly under the lens. Everything stacked on one vertical axis.
prompts.197: An optical polishing machine: a squat cylindrical machine base carrying a flat rotating lap plate, with a round glass lens blank held face down against the lap by a swinging overarm, and a small slurry nozzle on a bracket dripping onto the lap. Simple, low, and heavy.
prompts.201: A bridge-type coordinate measuring machine: a heavy flat granite table with a portal bridge spanning it on two legs, a vertical quill hanging from the crossbeam, and a slender stylus with a small ball tip at its lower end touching the top face of a machined part sitting on the table. Open, rectilinear, precise.

partPrompts.1: A tight coil of rolled metal strip standing on its edge, seen three-quarter: a wide cylindrical roll of thin sheet with the spiral clearly visible on the exposed end face and the loose outer end lifting away slightly. Beside it lie two short round billets. One bold simple silhouette, no machine, no tooling.
partPrompts.2: Three finished discrete metal parts arranged in a small group on a flat surface: a round flanged hub with a bored center, a bracket bent from flat plate, and a short toothed gear blank. Distinct simple shapes with clear gaps between them, no machine and no tooling.
partPrompts.3: Two flat rectangular plates lying edge to edge on a flat surface, joined along their single straight seam by a weld bead drawn as a continuous line of overlapping shallow ripples. Both plates are the same thickness and lie flush. Nothing above the plates, no torch and no machine.
partPrompts.4: A single round bar lying horizontally, its left half plain and its right half visibly coated in a darker even layer, with a clean straight boundary where the treatment stops partway along. One object, no tank, no bath and no equipment.
partPrompts.5: A round silicon wafer lying flat, seen three-quarter: a disc with a small flat notch at one edge and a regular grid of small square dies covering its face, with partial dies cut off around the rim. One object on a plain surface, no machine.
partPrompts.6: A lens barrel assembly standing upright on a flat surface: a short cylindrical metal mount, wider at the base, holding a glass lens at its open top, where the glass swells up out of the rim as a smooth shallow dome so the bulge is clearly visible in profile against the background. A stepped ring runs around the outside of the barrel. Beside it, well separated, a small solid triangular prism standing on one face. The domed glass and the triangular prism are the two shapes that must read; no flat rings, no holes, no annulus, no light rays, no machine.
partPrompts.7: A micrometer gauge closed around a small round part, seen three-quarter: a C-shaped frame with a knurled cylindrical barrel on one side and its two flat measuring faces touching the part from both sides. One tool, one part, nothing else.
